history.content: My sorghum plants stay short and yellow even though the rains are good, what is happening?

Next, bring back organic matter by applying manure, compost, or by leaving or burying the sorghum residues instead of burning them. After that, rotate with a legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. history.content: How do I manage an outbreak of peste des petits ruminants in my goats?

First, keep all your goats separated from the sick herd. Second, do not force any animal to move or give any milk. Third, keep any visitor away from the animals. Fourth, dispose of dead animals by burying them deep or burning them, and never sell or consume a sick animal. Finally, contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary immediately.

history.content: what tolerant cassava variety should I plant and when to sow

Also avoid planting sorghum late in the season because late sowing raises infection risk. If many plants are showing the virus, see ICAT to confirm and to obtain a tolerant variety.

The yellowing is caused by a nitrogen shortage in your sorghum, not by any virus. First, look at the leaves before buying any input; the uniform pale yellow on older lower leaves signals nitrogen deficiency. Second, restore organic matter by applying manure, compost, or burying residues instead of burning them, because mineral fertilizer alone will not work on exhausted soil. Third, add a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Fourth, request a soil check from ICAT to obtain the right dose for your plot. I cannot give you a precise fertilizer recommendation without that analysis.

history.content: My herd has sudden diarrhoea and many goats are dying quickly, almost all of them. What is happening?

draws.answer: The problem is leucaena poisoning caused by too much leucaena in the diet. Reduce leucaena to no more than a quarter to a third of the total ration and do not let it become the main feed. Blend the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to give the rumen enough roughage. Change the feed gradually over several days to let the animals adjust. Keep clean water available at all times and give a mineral or salt source. If the animals keep dying, see the veterinary service.

Your herd is infected by gall sickness caused by Anaplasma marginale. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can tell if it is gall sickness or redwater and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet that the urine colour is yellow-brown without red. Keep the sick animal in the shade, give it clean water, and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not only on the sick animal. The veterinary service will provide the needed treatment.

per_item.reference: These observations match PPR, peste des petits ruminants, a fast and highly contagious virus that hits goats hard. You must isolate every sick goat immediately and stop all movement of animals into or out of the herd. Do not sell or slaughter any goats for market while the disease is present, and make sure any carcasses are disposed of safely. Provide water and soft feed to the sick goats to support them. Then vaccinate all healthy and in-contact goats with the PPR vaccine on veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service IMMEDIATELY.

history.content: My goats are dying fast, they have fever, runny eyes and noses, and some have mouth sores, what is the problem?

Keep clean water and a mineral or salt source always available. If the goats keep dying or you see a swollen throat, see the veterinary service.

history.content: My sheep are coughing, have diarrhoea and some are dying fast, what should I do?

draws.answer: It is leucaena poisoning caused by leucaena consumption. First, cut the leucaena back so it forms only about a quarter to a third of the total ration and never let it be the main feed. Then blend the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to increase the amount of roughage. Introduce any feed change gradually over several days, avoiding a sudden switch. Provide constant clean water and a mineral or salt source. If the sheep keep losing appetite, drooling or developing a swollen throat, see the veterinary service.

Your sheep are afflicted by a tick-borne disease, either gall sickness or redwater, carried by Amblyomma variegatum or Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus ticks. Call the veterinary service today so they can determine which disease it is and supply the right drug and dose. Inform the vet that the urine colour is red to almost black, which indicates redwater, while yellow-brown urine would suggest gall sickness. Keep the sick sheep in the shade, ensure clean water is available, and avoid making it walk because it lacks red blood cells. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not just on the sick sheep, to prevent further spread. See the veterinary service the same day.

per_item.reference: Those are signs of cassava brown streak disease on cassava. First, take cuttings only from plants that look healthy and plant a variety that tolerates the disease. Next, pull out any cassava plants showing the yellow leaf veins or the brown corky rot in the roots and destroy them completely. Also, avoid moving any cuttings from fields where those symptoms appear. Finally, bring a sample to ITRA so they can confirm the presence of cassava brown streak disease, because root symptoms need checking.

history.content: My cassava leaves have yellow streaks on the veins and when I dig up the roots they are brown and corky. What should I do?

draws.answer: Those signs are cassava mosaic disease. Remove and destroy every plant showing the yellow streaks on the veins and the brown, corky lesions in the roots. For the next planting, take cuttings only from plants that appear healthy, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Use improved tolerant varieties obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and rotate the plot to a different area. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA is the service to contact.

Those signs indicate cassava mosaic disease, which cannot be cured with chemicals. First, uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly that spreads the virus. Next, for the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants, avoiding any mottled or deformed stems. Then, select an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and maintain a uniform, well-fed stand. If you need help distinguishing mosaic from bacterial blight, go to ICAT; for clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

per_item.reference: Striga, known locally as witchweed, can be managed by first feeding the soil with organic manure and a small amount of urea; this weakens the parasite and boosts sorghum health. Then pull the witchweed by hand before it flowers and burn the uprooted plants to prevent seed spread. Follow with a rotation or intercrop using a grain legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean to run down the seed bank. For severe infestations, see ICAT for tolerant varieties and a multi-year rotation plan.

history.content: What steps should I take against Striga hermonthica on my sorghum?

draws.answer: Striga hermonthica is the parasitic weed attacking your sorghum. First, sow your sorghum on rich, well-drained soil and perform the first weeding at the right time. Then, at about 30-35 days after sowing, treat the soil with 2-3 kg of urea per hectare, following the plan you have received from ICAT. This will keep the sorghum seedlings from touching the striga plant and letting it flower. When the sorghum reaches panicle initiation, roughly 30-45 days after sowing, pull out the striga plants from the field. To confirm the weed and get the proper urea dose, visit ICAT.

Striga hermonthica is the parasitic plant that takes root in sorghum and prevents the plant from bearing a good yield. Grow your sorghum on light, well-drained soil and sow seed that has been treated with a Fongorene-type product at six grams per kilogram of seed. Weed the field at two weeks and again three weeks after sowing. When the sorghum plants reach panicle initiation, treat with an approved seed protectant or inert material. For the correct current fungicide recommendation, go to ICAT.
